research_concepts: opponent next-possession PPP after offensive play type
AVOID label based on subsequent outcomes
methodological_questions: How to reliably identify opponent's next possession after a specific play in play-by-play data, handling transitions, end-of-quarter, and substitutions?
What are the statistical risks in using subsequent PPP to label plays as avoid, considering sample size, sparsity, and multiple testing across play types?
How to define own-sequence lags (next possession points) and handle censoring at end-of-game?
Can derived play-type labels be trusted given error in action-to-play mapping, and how does label noise affect outcome analysis?
What confounding factors (score differential, time remaining, opponent strength, lineup changes) must be addressed when linking plays to subsequent defensive outcomes?

historical_evidence.finding: Defensive scheme change within game and across games (inferred labels). Within-game change 319/523, cross-game 298/440, but near-uniform transition matrices consistent with label noise made the question untestable; limited by label/classification error.

Superstar sequential suppression: opponent play before the star. PUTBACK appeared as top suppressor for several stars (e.g., D. Mitchell d=-0.294, n_after=95), but no multiplicity correction, small n_after for many cells, and risk of drift nonstationarity; not a formal hypothesis test.

LLM / ex-ante usefulness of suppression context (leakage audit). Suppression label was mostly an RTM artifact due to selection on the outcome; remaining LLM edge not statistically retrievable after leakage correction. Label/classification error and RTM selection noted.

Gravity persistence: elite creator -> teammate PPP at lags 1-3. All 8 creators showed no lift at horizon=0; Jokic lag-1 ATT=+0.0282 CI[-0.043,+0.099] p=0.3779 with n=1880. Adequately powered null for own-sequence teammate PPP.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using inferred labels from play-by-play to detect defensive scheme change within/across games.
failed_approaches.why: Label/classification error produced near-uniform transition matrices that masked any real adjustment, making the question untestable.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Building a suppression-prediction label from outcome (PPP) and evaluating LLM usefulness.
failed_approaches.why: Label was an RTM artifact because it was selected on the outcome; the apparent signal vanished after accounting for leakage.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attempting to quantify opponent play-type suppression on star PPP without formal testing.
failed_approaches.why: Small effective sample sizes (n_after 32-95) for many cells and absence of multiplicity correction prevented a valid hypothesis test.

evidence_establishes: Outcome-derived labels (e.g., AVOID based on next-possession PPP) are susceptible to regression-to-the-mean artifacts and label noise, making them untrustworthy (FAM:SF-CHT-086, FAM:SF-APPA-005).

Own-sequence lag PPP after a specific action (elite creator) is essentially null even with large samples, suggesting any signal for own-sequence points after a play type is very small or absent (FAM:SF-APPS-074).
Studies that examine opponent next possession after a specific play type, without proper multiplicity correction, yield noisy results that cannot support rigorous inference (FAM:SF-APPA-050).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether opponent next-possession PPP after offensive play types (as distinct from opponent prior possession play types) shows meaningful variation that could drive an AVOID label.

That own-sequence PPP after an entire offensive play type (rather than a star's action) is null; the prior null was for teammate PPP after a star's signature action, which may not generalise to all play types.
own_inferences: Defining an AVOID label by the observed opponent next-possession PPP inherently selects extreme values; regression to the mean will cause those labels to be unreliable on new data, creating a self-fulfilling artifact similar to FAM:SF-CHT-086.
Play-type labels derived from the play-by-play are imperfect; misclassification will attenuate any true differences and can generate spurious patterns, as seen in FAM:SF-APPA-005.

Most offensive play types, especially those that might be candidates for AVOID, occur relatively infrequently, so the per-type sample of opponent next possessions will be too small to overcome noise from the highly variable single-possession PPP metric.

The null findings on own-sequence lags (FAM:SF-APPS-074) suggest that even if opponent next-possession effects exist, their magnitude is likely modest and could be easily obscured by confounding from game state, opponent strength, and lineup changes.
uncertainties: The exact misclassification rate of the derived play-type possession records is not documented for this specific graph database; some play types may be more reliably identified than others.
The optimal way to isolate the causal effect of a play on the next defensive possession is unresolved, particularly for possessions that end quarters or are followed by timeouts/substitutions.
No prior study has directly tested whether opponent next-possession PPP differs by offensive play type after adjustment for contextual factors, so the true effect size is unknown.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieval showed that outcome-based labeling (AVOID from PPP) reliably produces regression-to-the-mean artifacts (FAM:SF-CHT-086) and that label noise from play-by-play inference can render studies untestable (FAM:SF-APPA-005). Without this evidence, one might have underestimated the magnitude of the RTM problem and attempted a naïve AVOID-label analysis. The history directly warns against the label-first approach implied by the question.

blocking_constraints.text: Defining AVOID labels based on the opponent's next-possession PPP selects extreme outcomes; those labels will not replicate on new data, making any apparent pattern an artifact.
Play-type labels derived from play-by-play are imperfect; misclassification reduces signal-to-noise and can create spurious deficits or surpluses that mimic genuine play-type differences.
Many play types occur too rarely to produce reliable per-type opponent next-possession PPP estimates; the wide confidence intervals will preclude any confident AVOID designation.

prior_work.summary: Prior work shows that outcome-derived suppression/avoid labels are artifacts (RTM, label noise), and that own-sequence PPP lags after a star's action are null. It does not directly test whether opponent next-possession PPP after offensive play types is large enough to drive AVOID labels, but it strongly suggests the AVOID-label approach is unsound.

risks.text: AVOID labels selected on opponent next-possession PPP will regress to the mean; extreme labels are unlikely to generalise.
Misclassification of play types from the play-by-play adds noise and may invert or exaggerate differences.
Rare play types will have very few opponent next-possessions, producing high-variance PPP estimates.

Score differential, time remaining, opponent strength, lineup, and home/away all influence both play selection and subsequent defensive outcomes; failure to fully adjust will produce spurious associations.
Detecting a practically meaningful difference (e.g., 0.05 PPP) requires hundreds of observations per play type; many play types will fall below this threshold.
Testing tens of play types inflates the false discovery rate; unadjusted p-values will label some plays as AVOID purely by chance.
Single-possession PPP is a very noisy metric; true effects are easily lost in the within-possession variance.
Play-type effectiveness and defensive adjustments may change over the season and across playoff rounds, undermining a static analysis.
If the AVOID label is constructed using future data in the same game or season, the model could inadvertently incorporate information not available at the moment of the play.
The expected opponent PPP is near league average (~1.1); even a real effect will be a fraction of this, making it hard to separate from noise.

design.estimand: Causal effect of running offensive play type X (versus a reference set of plays) on the opponent's points per possession on the immediately following defensive possession, adjust for game context.
design.sample: All possessions from the 2022-23 through 2025-26 NBA regular seasons and playoffs for which (a) a single offensive play type can be assigned from the play-by-play, (b) the possession does not end a quarter (so an opponent next possession is observed), (c) garbage time (defined by win probability >0.95 or <0.05 in the fourth) is excluded, and (d) the defensive possession is not interrupted by a timeout or deliberate foul before the shot.
design.power: Power calculation: to detect a 0.05 PPP difference with 80% power and α=0.05 (two-sided), approximately 500 observations per play type are needed assuming a possession-level PPP standard deviation of ~1.1. Only play types meeting n≥500 in the training set will be tested; a separate holdout season (e.g., 2025-26) will be used for confirmatory analysis.
design.controls: Fixed effects for season, team (offense and defense), whether the previous possession was a made basket, turnover, or defensive rebound; current score margin (binned into -30 to +30 in 5-point increments); time remaining (period number and seconds remaining in period); defensive lineup strength (rolling net rating of the five players on the floor); offensive lineup strength; home/away; back-to-back indicator; starting or bench unit indicator.
design.falsification: 1. Test that play type does not predict own previous possession PPP (should be unrelated). 2. Permutation test: shuffle the play type labels within the same game segment and re-estimate the effects; the true effect size distribution should be centred at zero. 3. Placebo test: use opponent next-possession PPP lagged by two possessions (i.e., the possession after the next) as outcome; no effect should appear.
design.multiplicity: Adjust p-values across all tested play types using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate at 0.05.
design.decision_rule: A play type is flagged as a potential AVOID candidate only if (a) its adjusted p-value < 0.05, (b) the estimated opponent-next-PPP difference is positive and >0.05 PPP in the training set, and (c) the effect replicates in the holdout season with nominal p<0.05 (one-sided). The label 'AVOID' would then be assigned in future analysis based on these criteria, never on the raw outcome in the same sample.
design.data_version: NBA per-game play-by-play API data and derived play-type possession records as of 2026-06-19.

You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.

Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:

identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from

no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["opponent next-possession PPP after offensive play type", "own-sequence lag outcomes after play", "AVOID label based on subsequent outcomes", "play-type labeling from play-by-play", "possession-level outcome regression", "defensive matchup data quality"], "methodological_questions": ["How to reliably identify opponent's next possession after a specific play in play-by-play data, handling transitions, end-of-quarter, and substitutions?", "What are the statistical risks in using subsequent PPP to label plays as avoid, considering sample size, sparsity, and multiple testing across play types?", "How to define own-sequence lags (next possession points) and handle censoring at end-of-game?", "Can derived play-type labels be trusted given error in action-to-play mapping, and how does label noise affect outcome analysis?", "What confounding factors (score differential, time remaining, opponent strength, lineup changes) must be addressed when linking plays to subsequent defensive outcomes?"], "query": "Opponent next-possession PPP after running a specific play type as a driver for AVOID labels, own-sequence lags similarly matter, play-type labeling and data quality"}}

reasoning_details.text:
We are at Stage 1: retrieval. We need to read the research objective and data description, identify research concepts and methodological questions, and call retrieve_history.

The task: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter." So the research question is about whether opponent's points per possession (PPP) after a team runs a particular play type (play X) is large enough to influence labeling plays as "AVOID" (i.e., bad plays to avoid). Also, own-sequence lags similarly matter, meaning that the effect of running a play on subsequent possessions (like own next possession outcomes) is also important.

The area: play-type labeling and data quality. They have data from several NBA seasons up to 2025-26, with per-game files from NBA stats API including play-by-play, substitution rotation, starters, defensive matchup, box-score. Also derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database.

The research concepts: 
- Opponent next-possession PPP after a specific play type. So looking at the defensive outcome after an offensive play.
- Own-sequence lags: maybe own team's next possession outcome after running a play.
- AVOID labels: classifying plays as ones to avoid.
- Play-type labeling: assigning a play type to a possession based on action type, sub-type, etc.
- Data quality issues: because labeling is derived.

Methodological questions:
- How to measure opponent PPP after a play? Need to define possessions, identify opponent's next possession reliably. Data from play-by-play can identify possessions but there may be issues with clock, period changes, substitutions. 
- How to define "play X"? From derived play-type possession records. Might be based on play-by-play action types, but are those labels accurate? There's potential for label error.
- Statistical risks: sample size, multiple testing (many play types), sparsity for rare plays, confounding (e.g., the situation after a play might depend on score, time, opponent strength, etc.), leakage lookahead (if labeling uses future info), mechanical floor effects, RTM selection. 
- The task says "own-sequence lags similarly matter" so they want to examine lagged outcomes (like own next possession points) as well. So methodological question: how to define own-sequence lags in a game, handle end-of-quarter/game possessions where next possession might be far away, etc.

We should retrieve_history with these concepts and questions.

Note: the retrieve_history args: research_concepts (list of strings), methodological_questions (list of strings), query (natural language string). So we'll formulate.

I'll make the call.

We need to produce the final assessment. First, we will analyze retrieval results. We have four families: FAM:SF-APPA-005, FAM:SF-APPA-050, FAM:SF-CHT-086, FAM:SF-APPS-074. The research question: "Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter." So the idea is to use subsequent outcomes (opponent PPP next possession, and own team's next possession points) to label plays as "avoid" (presumably, if opponent scores well after the play, you should avoid it). The question is whether these subsequent PPPs are large enough to drive these AVOID labels. That seems to be about effect sizes, sample sizes, and reliability. Also, own-sequence lags similarly matter: maybe own next-possession points.

Now, historical evidence:

- FAM:SF-APPA-005: Defensive scheme change within game and across games (inferred labels). Status: untestable. Observed failure: label/classification error, near-uniform transition matrices consistent with label noise. Relevant? This is about inferences of defensive scheme changes from inferred labels. It highlights that inferred labels (like play types?) can be noisy, and label noise can make tests untestable. Since our question uses play-type labels and next-possession PPP, label error is a major risk. Shows that previous work with similar labeling was limited by label error. So we can cite this as evidence that label noise can render such studies untestable.

- FAM:SF-APPA-050: Superstar sequential suppression: opponent play before the star. Status: "not a hypothesis test". Objective: a specific opponent play type on the preceding possession suppresses each star's next-possession PPP. Result: some evidence like PUTBACK is top suppressor for many stars with n_after 32-95. But no multiplicity correction, small sample, drift risk. Not a hypothesis test. This is similar to the question about opponent next-possession PPP depending on the play you run. It's also about opponents' next possession after a specific play. However, that study looked at suppression of star's PPP by prior opponent play type, not after the star's own team ran a play. But the methodological issues are similar: small n_after for many play types, no multiplicity correction, risk of drift. So we can use this as evidence that small sample sizes for specific play types make it hard to detect effects with adequate power. This is relevant because our question would examine opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X; each play type will have some number of occurrences, likely small for many, leading to exposure sparsity, sample size/power issues. So that's a failed approach? It was not a hypothesis test, but it showed that approach yields small n and no correction.

- FAM:SF-CHT-086: LLM / ex-ante usefulness of suppression context (leakage audit). Status: artifact. Observed failure: label is mostly an RTM artifact, label selected on outcome, remaining LLM edge not statistically retrievable. Also related to APPA-005. This is about using outcome to define a "suppression" label and then trying to predict it, leading to RTM. Similarly, if we try to define AVOID labels based on opponent next-possession PPP (outcome), we risk regression to the mean. So this is directly relevant: labeling based on outcome yields artifacts. So that's a clear risk: RTM_SELECTION, LABEL_ERROR. So this family shows that using outcome-derived labels (like AVOID) is likely an artifact.

- FAM:SF-APPS-074: Gravity persistence: elite creator -> teammate PPP at lags 1-3. Status: rejected. Hypothesis: After elite creator's signature action, teammates score more on next possessions with same lineup. Result: null on teammate PPP, no lift at any lag. This is about own-sequence lags: next possession PPP for own team. It shows that own-sequence lags after specific player actions did not yield a detectable effect, even with large sample sizes. This suggests that own-sequence lags as an outcome may be null, or at least not large enough. That's directly relevant to the question's "own-sequence lags similarly matter" part. So that could indicate that own-sequence PPP after a play type probably doesn't matter, or that effect sizes are tiny. This can inform our predicted outcome: likely null or very small effect. The evidence from that study: null result with large samples (Jokic lag-1 n=1880, Giannis n=1804). So if we try to use own-sequence PPP to label plays, we might find nothing.

Now, step 4: Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches. We'll include all four families.

Step 5: What does historical evidence establish and not establish? Evidence establishes that label noise and RTM can produce artifacts when using outcome-derived labels (SF-CHT-086, SF-APPA-005). It establishes that studying opponent next possession after a specific play type with small n_after yields low power and lacks multiplicity correction (SF-APPA-050). It establishes that own-sequence lags (team PPP after specific actions) are essentially null even with large samples (SF-APPS-074). It does not establish directly whether opponent next-possession PPP after play types can drive AVOID labels. But the prior work on suppression contexts and label error strongly suggests that such labeling would suffer from RTM and label noise. Also, own-sequence lags appear to be null, so that part of the hypothesis is likely unsupported.

Step 6: Assess testability. We need to assign a p_testable probability. The data includes play-by-play, derived play-type possession records, etc. But the question as posed is about whether these outcome-based labels are "large enough to drive AVOID labels." That's essentially a labeling exercise. The methodological risks: RTM from using outcome to define labels, label noise, sparsity for many play types, confounding (score, time, opponent strength, lineup). The prior evidence shows that similar studies were untestable or null. I'd say testability is low because of label noise and RTM; but perhaps one could test whether differences in opponent next-possession PPP by play type are statistically significant after adjusting for confounders, and then whether those differences are large enough to be actionable. However, the question as framed is more about whether it's "large enough to drive AVOID labels," which implies using the outcome to decide labels, which is circular. The study would likely be an artifact. So p_testable might be low, say 0.2, with blocking constraints: RTM_SELECTION, LABEL_ERROR, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY.

Step 7: Identify methodological risks and confounders. List risks: RTM_SELECTION (deriving labels from outcome), LABEL_ERROR (play-type misclassification), EXPOSURE_SPARSITY (small samples for rare plays), CONFOUNDING (game context, opponent quality, score differential, lineup, home/away, fatigue), MULTIPLE_TESTING (many play types), SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, BASE_RATE (expected PPP is around 1.0, effects small), MEASURE_RELIABILITY (PPP on single possession noisy), LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD (if using future data to label plays in the same game, you'd be using knowledge of the game outcome if not careful? But that's about labeling; potential for leakage if you use whole season to label, but that's less of an issue for RTM than for prediction. But still a concern: using outcome to label is RTM). Also, MECHANICAL_FLOOR: PPP bounded non-negative, and opponent possession after a play might be mechanically correlated if the play ends a quarter or leads to a turnover, etc. Need to handle that.

Step 8: Final research decision. Likely do_not_proceed because of high risk of artifact (RTM, label noise), low power for rare plays, and prior evidence that own-sequence lags are null, and that outcome-derived labels produce artifacts. However, maybe we could proceed with changes if we restrict to frequent play types, avoid outcome-based labeling and instead ask a predictive question: "Does play type predict opponent next-possession PPP after controlling for context?" That would be a different question. But the question specifically is about whether it's large enough to drive AVOID labels, which implies using the outcome to label. That's inherently an artifact-prone design. So I'd decide do_not_proceed.

Step 9: How historical evidence changed the decision: The retrieval showed that similar labeling attempts ended as artifacts or null, confirming the risks.

Now, fill in the output schema.

First, research_concepts: from stage 1, we can list the concepts we used. I'll restate them: opponent next-possession PPP after offensive play type, own-sequence lag outcomes, AVOID label based on subsequent outcomes, play-type labeling from play-by-play, possession-level outcome regression, defensive matchup data quality.

methodological_questions: same as earlier.

historical_evidence: I'll list the four records with their status and finding. For APPA-005: status "untestable", finding "Defensive scheme change within game and across games (inferred labels). Within-game change 319/523, cross-game 298/440, but transition matrices near-uniform, consistent with label noise; untestable due to label/classification error." I'll paraphrase concisely. Actually, I'll quote the document's observed_hypothesis and observed_result and auto_failure_mechanism. I need to keep the status exactly as recorded: "untestable" for that record. So for FAM:SF-APPA-005, status "untestable", finding: "The study found frequent inferred scheme changes but the near-uniform transition matrices suggested label noise, making the question untestable (label/classification error)." I'll craft.

For FAM:SF-APPA-050, status "not a hypothesis test". finding: "Superstar sequential suppression: opponent play before the star. PUTBACK was top suppressor for several stars (e.g. Mitchell PPP diff -0.294, n_after=95), but no multiplicity correction and small n_after for many cells, risk of drift nonstationarity. Not formally a hypothesis test." That covers it.

For FAM:SF-CHT-086, status "artifact". finding: "LLM/ex-ante usefulness of suppression context: Label was mostly an RTM artifact; selection on outcome introduced label error and RTM, and remaining LLM edge was not statistically retrievable."

For FAM:SF-APPS-074, status "rejected". finding: "Gravity persistence: after elite creator's signature action, teammates' PPP at lags 1-3. All 8 creators horizon=0. Lag-1 Jokic ATT=+0.0282 CI[-0.043,+0.099] p=0.3779, null result adequately powered (Jokic lag-1 n=1880). Own-sequence PPP lift absent."

failed_approaches: I'll identify approaches that failed. FAM:SF-APPA-005: using inferred labels for scheme change failed due to label error. FAM:SF-CHT-086: outcome-derived suppression labels led to RTM artifact. FAM:SF-APPA-050: not a hypothesis test, but approach of small n for opponent next possession after specific play type without multiplicity correction failed to yield a rigorous test. Also, FAM:SF-APPS-074: the attempt to find teammate PPP lift after star action failed (null result), but that was an adequately powered null, not a failure of approach. So I'll include the first three as failed approaches.

evidence_establishes: - Outcome-derived labels (like AVOID based on subsequent PPP) are susceptible to RTM and label noise, making tests of their predictive value artifact-prone (FAM:SF-CHT-086, FAM:SF-APPA-005). - Own-sequence lag PPP after specific plays is effectively null even with large samples (FAM:SF-APPS-074). - Opponent next-possession PPP after specific opponent play types has sample-size constraints and lacks formal hypothesis testing (FAM:SF-APPA-050).

evidence_does_not_establish: - Whether opponent next-possession PPP after specific offensive play types (as opposed to opponent plays) shows meaningful variation that could drive avoid recommendations. The studies did not examine offensive play types directly. - The own-sequence null was for teammate PPP after star actions, not for the team's PPP after specific offensive play types.

own_inferences: - Using next-possession PPP to label plays as "avoid" would introduce a severe RTM problem because the label is defined by the very outcome one might try to predict; any extreme value would regress on subsequent observations. - Play-type classification from play-by-play is imperfect; label noise would attenuate any true signal and could create spurious patterns. - For rare play types, the number of samples would be too small to reliably estimate opponent next-possession PPP after controlling for game context, leading to overfitting and lack of generalizability. - The lack of own-sequence effect in previous work suggests that even if opponent effects exist, they may be small and confounded.

uncertainties: - The exact degree of label error in the derived play-type possession records from the play-by-play is unknown but likely substantial for some play types. - The optimum methodology for isolating the causal effect of a play on the next defensive possession is unclear (e.g., handling end-of-quarter, timeouts, substitution patterns). - No study has tested the specific hypothesis that opponent next-possession PPP differs by offensive play type (as opposed to opponent prior play type).

historical_effect: changed_decision: "yes" - explanation: The retrieval revealed prior instances where outcome-derived labels led to artifacts (RTM) and label noise made testing impossible, confirming the high risk of using PPP to define AVOID labels. Moreover, the null finding for own-sequence lags suggests low signal. Without this evidence, one might have underestimated the RTM problem and attempted a naive analysis.

testability: p_testable: 0.15 (i.e., low probability that a well-powered, unbiased test can be conducted). Blocking constraints:
